title: THE BIBLE ACTUALLY TELLS A HUSBAND TO DELIGHT IN HIS WIFE’S BODY — But Proverbs 5 Is Saying Something Far Deeper
paragraphs: THE BIBLE ACTUALLY TELLS A HUSBAND TO DELIGHT IN HIS WIFE’S BODY — But Proverbs 5 Is Saying Something Far Deeper

Proverbs 5 does not blush when it speaks about marital desire. God created covenant love, and Scripture refuses to surrender something beautiful to a culture that has distorted it. But read the whole passage before you reduce it to sex—because beneath these intimate words is a warning about temptation, faithfulness, secrecy, consequences, and a God who sees every road we take.
There are verses some Christians almost whisper.
Not because they are ashamed of Scripture.
But because they are surprised Scripture says them at all.
Proverbs 5:18–19 is one of those passages.
“Rejoice with the wife of thy youth.”
Then Solomon becomes even more intimate.
He speaks of the husband being satisfied by his wife’s breasts and continually captivated by her love.
Yes.
That is in the Bible.

And before someone turns it into a crude joke, before someone weaponizes it against a spouse, and before someone concludes Christianity considers the human body dirty, we need to hear what Proverbs is actually saying.
Because Proverbs 5 is not pornography wearing religious clothing.
It is wisdom defending covenant intimacy from the destruction of adultery.
And its message is far bigger than physical attraction.
The chapter begins with a father pleading with his son to pay attention to wisdom.
“My son, attend unto my wisdom, and bow thine ear to my understanding.”
Why?
Because temptation can sound beautiful before it becomes devastating.
Proverbs describes forbidden sexual temptation with frightening realism: the lips of the forbidden woman drip honey, and her speech is smoother than oil.
At first, everything tastes sweet.
Then comes the sentence temptation never puts in the advertisement:
“But her end is bitter as wormwood.”
That is how sin works.
It shows you the beginning.
God warns you about the ending.
Sin shows the hotel room.
God sees the marriage collapsing afterward.
Sin shows the message notification.
God sees the spouse eventually discovering it.
Sin shows the excitement.
God sees the children crying.
Sin shows the secret.
God sees what the secret is turning you into.

And please understand the passage carefully: Proverbs is giving a father’s warning to a son within its literary setting. It is not teaching that women are inherently seductive or responsible for male sin. Elsewhere Scripture condemns adultery regardless of who commits it and calls both men and women to sexual faithfulness.
The real enemy being exposed here is unfaithfulness.
The frightening ability of desire to detach itself from covenant.
So Scripture gives a startling alternative.
“Drink waters out of thine own cistern, and running waters out of thine own well.”
That language is poetic.
Intimate.
Deliberate.
Then comes Proverbs 5:18:
יְהִי־מְקוֹרְךָ בָרוּךְ וּשְׂמַח מֵאֵשֶׁת נְעוּרֶךָ
Yehi-meqorkha varukh, u-semach me’eshet ne’urekha.
The central thought is beautifully rendered:
“Let your fountain be blessed, and rejoice in the wife of your youth.”
That Hebrew verb translated “rejoice” is שָׂמַח — samach.
Rejoice.
Be glad.
Take joy.
Marriage, in biblical wisdom, was never supposed to become merely two exhausted people sharing bills, responsibilities, children, schedules, and a surname.
God permits joy.
God created affection.
God created attraction.
God created the human body.
And within faithful marital covenant, Scripture does not treat sexual intimacy as something filthy that holy people reluctantly tolerate.
Proverbs actually celebrates marital delight.
Then verse 19 becomes even more explicit:
אַיֶּלֶת אֲהָבִים וְיַעֲלַת־חֵן דַּדֶּיהָ יְרַוֻּךָ בְכָל־עֵת בְּאַהֲבָתָהּ תִּשְׁגֶּה תָמִיד

The imagery describes the wife as a loving deer, a graceful doe, and says, in straightforward terms, that her breasts should satisfy her husband and that he should continually be captivated by her love.
Do not miss the last word.
Love.
This is not permission for a husband to treat his wife as an object.
This is not biblical authorization for coercion.
It does not mean a wife’s body belongs to a husband in the sense that her dignity, wellbeing, or personhood can be ignored.
The woman being described is not pornography.
She is his wife.
His covenant companion.
Someone to be loved, honored, cherished, protected, known, and delighted in.
The New Testament makes that responsibility unmistakable.
“Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it.”
Read that again before demanding anything from your wife.
As Christ loved the church.
How did Christ love?
By taking.
Or by giving Himself?
Biblical headship never gives a man permission to become selfish.
It gives him a cross.
Ephesians 5:28 goes even further:
“So ought men to love their wives as their own bodies.”
So when Proverbs tells a husband to delight in his wife, the larger biblical picture will never permit him to separate desire from sacrificial love.
Her body is not a product.
Her affection is not payment.
Her intimacy is not a commodity.
She is an image-bearer of God.
And Christian marital intimacy belongs inside a relationship shaped by fidelity, tenderness, honor, mutual care, and love.
But there is another side of Proverbs 5 that we desperately need to hear.
Because immediately after celebrating marital delight, Solomon asks:
“And why wilt thou, my son, be ravished with a strange woman, and embrace the bosom of a stranger?”
In other words:
Why abandon covenant water while dying of thirst beside your own well?
Why trade something sacred for something secret?
Why sacrifice years of trust for minutes of excitement?
Why gamble your marriage for a screen?
Why give another person emotional territory that belongs inside your covenant?
Why keep deleting conversations you would be terrified for your spouse to read?
Why call it harmless when you know you are hiding it?
Somebody reading this has crossed a line already.
Maybe nobody knows.
Your spouse does not know.
Your church does not know.
Your children do not know.
Your friends would never suspect it.
Maybe there has been no physical affair.
But there is someone you think about too much.
Someone whose messages make something inside you come alive.
Someone you tell things you stopped telling your spouse.
Maybe it is pornography.
Maybe secret flirting.
Maybe emotional infidelity.
Maybe memories of somebody from years ago that you keep feeding.
Maybe you have become addicted to looking at bodies belonging to people whose names you do not even know.
And you have been telling yourself:
Nobody is getting hurt.
Then Proverbs 5:21 arrives like footsteps in a silent hallway:
“For the ways of man are before the eyes of the LORD, and he pondereth all his goings.”
Nobody knows?
God does.
That should frighten the unrepentant heart.
But for the person ready to repent, it can also become the beginning of hope.
Because the God who sees the hidden road is also the God who calls sinners home.
Christianity does not teach that sexual sin is uniquely beyond forgiveness.
Jesus Christ came for sinners.
The Gospel is not God waiting for clean people to approach Him.
The Gospel is the holy Son of God coming for people who could never clean themselves.
At the cross, Jesus carried sin and shame.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose again.
And forgiveness is not found by pretending you never fell.
It is found in Christ.
Repentance does not mean merely feeling terrible because you were caught.
Repentance turns.
It brings darkness into light.
It stops defending what God calls sin.
It stops asking, “How much can I get away with?”
And begins asking:
“Jesus, what needs to die in me so I can walk faithfully with You?”
Maybe your marriage has grown cold.
That does not justify adultery.
Maybe intimacy has become difficult.
That does not justify pornography.
Maybe you feel rejected.
That does not authorize betrayal.
Maybe there are serious wounds between you and your spouse.
Those wounds may require honest conversations, pastoral wisdom, counseling, patience, boundaries, medical help, repentance, forgiveness, or long seasons of rebuilding.
But secret sin will not heal a wounded marriage.
It simply creates another wound.
And perhaps this is where Proverbs 5 becomes unexpectedly tender.
“Rejoice in the wife of your youth.”
There is something almost heartbreaking about that phrase.
The wife of your youth.
Remember her?
Remember him?
Remember when you could talk for hours?
Remember when holding hands meant something?
Remember when you noticed each other?
Before mortgages.
Before sleepless nights.
Before children.
Before disappointments.
Before arguments accumulated like boxes nobody wanted to unpack.
Before the phones entered the bedroom.
Before work followed you home.
Before familiarity quietly became neglect.
Some marriages do not collapse because somebody woke up wanting to destroy them.
Sometimes they starve slowly.
One unanswered conversation at a time.
One withheld apology at a time.
One evening of choosing the screen instead of the person beside you.
One unresolved resentment.
One secret comparison.
One flirtation.
One click.
One lie.
One more night saying, “We’ll talk tomorrow.”
Until two people who once could not stop talking can lie inches apart and feel miles away.
Maybe Proverbs 5 is calling some husbands and wives back before the funeral.
Not merely back to sex.
Back to each other.
Look at your spouse again.
Listen again.
Laugh again.
Pray together again.
Date each other again.
Become curious again.
Apologize without adding “but.”
Forgive where forgiveness is possible.
Get help where the damage is deeper than the two of you know how to repair.
And do not compare the ordinary, unfiltered human being who has carried life beside you with carefully selected images designed to capture your attention.
Your spouse is real.
Real bodies age.
Real bodies change.
Real bodies carry scars.
Real bodies gain weight and lose weight.
Real bodies become tired.
Real bodies get sick.
Real bodies carry children, stress, grief, hormones, years, and stories.
Covenant love learns something lust never can:
How to keep seeing beauty after novelty disappears.
And perhaps that is one reason Scripture can speak so freely about delight while remaining completely opposed to lustful exploitation.
Biblical marital desire says:
I delight in you within faithful love.
Lust says:
I consume you for myself.
Those are not the same thing.
One sees a person.
The other eventually sees a product.
One belongs to covenant.
The other is never satisfied.
One learns gratitude.
The other keeps scrolling.
And if you have already failed here, hear this carefully.
Your failure does not become holy because you rename it.
But neither is your failure greater than the grace of Jesus Christ.
The woman caught in adultery encountered Jesus.
The sexually broken encountered Jesus.
The ashamed encountered Jesus.
The religiously proud encountered Jesus too.
Jesus did not redefine sin to make sinners comfortable.
And He did not require sinners to repair themselves before they could come near.
Grace does something far more astonishing.
Grace meets sinners in truth...
and calls them into a different life.
That is why our message will always be:
Not from scandal to pretending.
Not from scandal to public image management.
Not from scandal to “everybody does it.”
Not from scandal to permanent condemnation.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not have to confess the details publicly. But do not keep hiding from Christ.
Somebody silently reading may desperately need evidence that repentance, forgiveness, rebuilding, and grace are still possible.
And if you know a husband, wife, engaged couple, struggling believer, or even someone quietly losing a battle nobody else knows about, send this to them.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God—it does not.
Jesus Christ cannot be bought.
Grace cannot be purchased.
Salvation is God's gift, received through faith.
Support should flow from gratitude to God, never guilt or spiritual pressure.
If you want to support Gospel Warrior and continue walking with this community:
There may be a night when temptation speaks more loudly than wisdom, and you will need to remember where that road ends.
Send it privately to somebody trying to rebuild a marriage.
And tonight, if you are married, perhaps put the phone down.
Look at the person beside you.
Not as an accessory.
Not as a body you are entitled to.
Not as the younger version of themselves you wish you could recover.
Look at the person who has walked through years with you.
And remember:
The world will teach you to chase what is new.
Pornography will teach you to consume what is available.
Adultery will promise excitement while hiding the bill.
But wisdom whispers something different:
Rejoice in the one to whom you made your covenant.
And if you have shattered that covenant, do not mistake the shattered pieces for the end of your story.
Bring your sin into the light.
Repent.
Seek Christ.
Tell the truth.
Accept the consequences truth may bring.
Get wise help.
Begin rebuilding what can be rebuilt.
Because the Gospel was never a story about people who never became scandalous.
It is the story of a Savior powerful enough to redeem sinners.
The secret that could have buried your story may become the very place where, through repentance and grace, Jesus begins writing truth across the ruins.
